newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Sierra Leone rebel chief to visit base on Friday.
newsitem.headline: Sierra Leone rebel chief to visit base on Friday.

text.p: Sierra Leone rebel leader Foday Sankoh, who has been in Ivory Coast since March, said on Wednesday he would return to consult his guerrillas this week ahead of an expected peace deal with the government.
"I should travel on Friday. I am going to consult my people on this peace accord -- whether I can get a mandate to sign it," Sankoh told Reuters in the Ivorian commercial capital Abidjan.
Government officials in Sierra Leone confirmed that President Ahmad Tejan Kabbah had approved the Revolutionary United Front (RUF) leader's visit.
Officials of the International Committee of the Red Cross said the organisation had been asked to arrange transport for Sankoh and his party from Ivory Coast on Friday.
"Corporal Sankoh will land in the country with a delegation from the Organisation of African Unity and the Commonwealth," a senior governmenmt official told Reuters in Freetown.
Sankoh said Kabbah had given assurances to him and mediator Ivory Coast for his security during the visit of about a week.
"Kabbah called me this afternoon. He wants to get his combatants to observe a ceasefire," Sankoh said.
Diplomats said Sankoh in turn had given an undertaking to the Ivorian government, the OAU and the United Nations that he would sign a final accord to end almost six years of civil war.
Asked to confirm remarks by Sierra Leone officials that an accord would be signed before Christmas, Sankoh said:
"Signing is not the problem. To implement is the problem."
He cited Angola where a 1991 accord to end 20 years of civil war broke down over elections forming part of the deal.
He struck a conciliatory note over the contentious issue of mercenaries from private South African firm Executive Outcomes, brought in to help the beleaguered army combat RUF in May 1985.
RUF and the government agreed to extend a temporary truce last March but Ivorian-mediated negotiations for a full accord broke down in May partly over RUF demands that the South Africans leave.

"We are not afraid of Executive Outcomes. If there is really a need for peace, that's not a problem for RUF," he said. "We maintain that there is no place for foreign troops in Sierra Leone, but if we are interested in peace that should not be in the way."
RUF took up arms in March 1991 and its guerrilla campaign has wrecked Sierra Leone's economy based on mining of bauxite, rutile, diamonds and gold and the growing of cocoa and coffee.

At the height of the war, guerrillas cut access to much of the interior and were attacking close to the capital by early 1995 despite the presence of Nigerian and Guinean troops backing the government army.

Fighting has intensified in the past two months despite the temporary ceasefire with a civilian militia drawn from Kamajor traditional hunters, which is allied with the army, overrunning major RUF bases.
RUF's only remaining stronghold appears to be around the eastern town of Kailahun, where Sankoh launched his campaign.
